findings.text: Within the first paragraph a newcomer learns what Athena is, who it is for and what problem it solves. The 'what is it' and 'why it matters' questions are answered at once.
findings.source: Header lede: "Athena is an open-source system, written in Rust, that turns a short request into a change to a code repository... It solves the problem of AI edits that arrive unreviewed and unaccountable."

findings.text: The page explains why a site about Athena is mostly about another project, firstmate. Without this, the title "Athena explains how firstmate handles work" would confuse a reader who has never heard of firstmate.
findings.source: Header lede: "A study is Athena's written reading of another software project... Athena made this study of firstmate to show that it can read an unfamiliar project and explain it"

findings.text: The next step is concrete: prerequisites, a clone command, an install command and a first request to try. The header also links straight to this section.
findings.source: Next steps: "Before installing, have git 2.40 or later, a C linker, curl, and either Claude Code or npm" / "./setup.sh" / "athena ask \"add a changelog\""

findings.text: The main thing Athena promises (one model does the work, another checks it, and costs are recorded) is never shown. The page shows only the claim-tracing side, so a newcomer has to install Athena on trust to see the core product.
findings.source: Header lede: "get back a commit they can trace to the request, the models, the cost and the verdict"

findings.text: This link is meant for the project owner, but it sits in the header next to the newcomer's next step. A first-time visitor may think it applies to them.
findings.source: Header: "Owner view: proposals waiting for your decision."

findings.text: Most of the page is a detailed state-machine reading of firstmate that is far more than a newcomer needs to judge Athena. The "Start here" section and the glossary help, but the page is long and dense.
findings.source: Sections "Counters" and "Transitions" (e.g. "places-held, changed by transitions t1, t3, t4, t9, t11")

findings.text: The page is open about its limits: nothing was run, and every claim comes from reading the source. That builds trust in how Athena reports its own evidence.
findings.source: Limits of this study, f1: "no failure or retry edge was observed; every claim is marked read."

findings.text: This is an internal detail that tells a newcomer nothing useful. It points to a folder they cannot see from the page.
findings.source: About this page: "the name of the folder under studies/ that holds the data this page is generated from"
